messages.content: I'm prototyping a tiny library catalog in Jac. Model each book as a node with a title, publication year, and an availability flag — the year should default to 0 when unknown and books should be available by default. Then write a librarian walker that starts at root, walks the shelf, and prints every book with its IN/OUT status.

I'm marking out a hiking trail in Jac as a chain of plain waypoints between the trailhead and the summit — the waypoints themselves don't need to hold any data at all. Give me a hiker walker that travels the trail and counts how many waypoints it passes, printing each stop number along the way and a completion line once it has passed enough of them.

Help me build a vet-clinic round in Jac. Pets are nodes with a name, species, and whether they need a vaccine today. A vet walker should keep its own list of patient names and count of shots given as it moves from pet to pet; afterwards I want to read those numbers straight off the spawned walker instance and print a summary.

I'm building an office tower tour in Jac. Floors are nodes holding their number and department. Write a tour-guide walker that announces the tour name when starting at root, then lets each floor's own ability print its stop as the walk continues up the building.

I'm making a tiny dungeon crawler in Jac. Rooms are chained nodes and one special room holds the treasure. A hunter walker should check rooms one by one while counting how many it has seen, and terminate the entire search immediately when it finds the treasure room — rooms past the vault must never be visited.

In my restaurant recommender, restaurants are nodes with a name, cuisine, and rating. I want one finder walker that takes a minimum rating as a spawn parameter rather than hardcoding it. Spawn it twice from root — once at 4.5+ for date night, once at 3.5+ for casual lunch — and print the matches from each pass.

I'm doing a warehouse stock take in Jac. Stock items are nodes with a SKU and a quantity. A counter walker should report each shelf quantity during its sweep, and the main block should read result.reports afterwards to print the per-item counts, the total units in the warehouse, and the smallest shelf count.

I'm building an alumni mentorship network in Jac. Mentor relationships are typed edges carrying the year each mentorship started. Create several mentorships between alumni, then write a finder walker that traverses only Mentor edges and filters on the start year so it can list everyone mentored since a given year.

Model mutual friendships in a small neighborhood for me: houses are nodes and buddy edges are bidirectional, created in a single statement. To prove the link really points both ways, spawn a separate greeter walker at each of the two houses and show that each reaches the other with forward traversal only — just make sure they can't bounce back and forth forever.

I'm encoding a family tree in Jac with ParentOf edges pointing from parents to children. Starting from someone in the middle generation, write a genealogy walker that visits that person's parents by walking incoming edges, then lists everyone directly linked in either direction, and stops once done.

Help me encode a CS curriculum in Jac: prerequisite edges form a chain built in one chained statement, and a lab course is co-requisite with its lecture via a bidirectional edge. A degree planner walker should skip courses the student already completed, note any co-requisite partners it meets along the way, and finish as soon as the senior capstone gets scheduled, reporting the planned credit total.

Model hospital ward doors for our ICU and General wards: when a nurse or doctor badges in, print their badge ID; family visitors trigger no ward response at all. Track how many wards each person entered during their shift.

Guests at our hotel walk past service desks (spa session, room-service dinner, express laundry); each desk adds its price to whichever guest is currently passing by. Print each charge as it happens and what each guest owes at checkout.

In our warehouse simulation, packing stations announce which robot they are serving while robots announce each station they stop at. Count stops per robot and boxes packed per station across a three-station line.

Crawl a small social graph: for each profile list who they timed-follow and what they posted, stamping how long each timed follow has been active during edge traversal itself, and never crawl the same profile twice even though some profiles are reachable by several paths.

Simulate a day at the midway: riders too short for the Viper coaster are turned away for the rest of their outing, rides award fun points, and food stalls and gift shops ring up purchases with receipts. Summarize fun points and spending for one tall and one short guest.

Model a city as stations connected to hotels and attractions, each attraction carrying a star rating. From every station, shortlist only the attractions (ignore hotels) and then only those rated 4 stars or higher, and print the final itinerary.
Given a co-authorship graph of researchers, suggest collaboration contacts for each researcher: people exactly two co-authored links away who are neither themselves nor direct co-authors already.

We run several depots that each serve a set of stores. Instead of checking depots one by one, anchor one combined query from the whole list of depot nodes at once, find every store within reach, and flag the ones whose stock has dropped below 20 units.

Print a fare board for our flight network. The flights themselves carry the data -- flight number and ticket price -- so read the connections themselves rather than just the destination airports, and list every departure from each airport with its fare.

Simulate contact tracing from patient zero through a network of contacts. The outbreak should spread wave by wave: everyone exposed in a wave gets contacted before the next wave starts. Print the contact sequence so the level-by-level order is evident.

I'm building a professional networking tool. When a user picks two people, I want the shortest chain of introductions between them, where each hop is a direct connection. Please give me a full program that builds a sample network and prints the introduction chain from one person to another.

I'm putting together a build system and need to catch circular dependencies before they cause infinite rebuilds. My modules each list the modules they depend on, and if you can get from a module back to itself by following dependencies, that's a bug worth reporting together with the exact cycle path. A runnable example with a deliberately broken graph would be great.

I'm modeling a vending machine controller for a hardware simulator. It has states like idle, waiting, and vend, and inputs like inserting a coin or pressing a button move it between them. I'd like to feed in a sequence of inputs and print which state we end in, following the matching transition for each input step by step.

I need a scheduler for our CI pipeline. Tasks have durations, some cannot start until others finish, and I want a valid execution order that respects all prerequisites plus the total time if tasks run one after another. If there is a cycle among the remaining tasks it should say so instead of getting stuck silently.

I'm playing with a knowledge graph of people, companies and cities connected by relations like works-at, lives-in and headquartered-in. From one person I want to answer questions like where their coworkers live, which companies are based in their own city, and which colleagues joined recently. A runnable demo answering several such multi-hop questions from a sample graph would help a lot.

I've got a family tree where each person links to their children. For a given person I want to enumerate ancestors by generation - parents first, then grandparents - walking against the direction of the links. A program that prints each generation separately for a three-generation family would be perfect.

I'm writing checkout logic for an online store. The cart holds different kinds of products - paper and digital books, electronics with warranties, clothing - and each kind has its own rules around shipping and handling. I'd like one checkout routine that reacts to each product's concrete type appropriately and prints an itemized receipt with subtotal, shipping and total.

I'm generating mazes for a puzzle game and need a solver. The maze is a grid of open cells surrounded by walls, with a marked entrance and exit, and the solver should probe paths depth-first - pushing deeper before backing up - until it reaches the exit, then report the route it took.

For our club tournament app I need to compute results through a single-elimination bracket. Seeded players meet in quarter-finals, winners advance toward the final, and in every match the higher-rated participant wins. Print each match's winner as it gets decided and crown the champion at the end.

I'm writing a little notes-and-tasks service in Jac that I'll serve with `jac start`. I want each logged-in user's tasks to live on their own private root, so creation should go through a private walker that lands on the authenticated user's root automatically. Show me the create side: spawn it twice and then list what landed under root.

For my task service I want a listing endpoint that returns every todo as one JSON array rather than a stream of partial results: collect during the walk and send everything back in a single report at the end, marked private so each user only ever sees their own graph. Seed a few todos in an entry block so the file also runs standalone.

My task app needs an edit endpoint. Clients only keep the id that creation reported back, so write a private walker that takes a jid string plus new title and done values, walks the caller's root until the jid matches, mutates the node in place, and stops early. A bogus id should simply produce no report.

I'm prototyping an event page in Jac and want a guestbook that works over HTTP without me writing route handlers. Two public walkers: one signs the guestbook, one reads the latest entries. Over `jac start` the walker fields should become the request body and the reports the response -- but keep an entry block so it runs standalone too.

For my reading-club site I want an anonymous poll -- no login, just tap a book title. One public walker sets up the options, another records a vote against a counter node, and a third reports tallies as the response. Simulate a few clicks locally so the file works without a server.

This is the reader half of my micro-blog: any caller, even anonymous, lists posts off the shared public graph in creation order. No auth needed since the commons floor lets everyone reach it and authors grant their posts readable. Include the publisher walker so the file runs standalone.

For my reports module the rule is: published reports are world-readable, unpublished ones fall back to whatever per-instance grants say. Define the archetype hook to return a READ level when published and None otherwise, so drafts stay closable but owners can still share them selectively. Add a publish walker that flips the flag and drops the now-redundant grant.

## Summary

The `pipeline:` field on a flowgroup does three jobs at once, with no way to separate them:

2. **Generated-code location** — the folder under `generated/<env>/<pipeline>/` the flowgroup's `.py` file is written to.
3. **Bundle resource identity** — the `resources/lhp/<pipeline>.pipeline.yml` file generated for it.

That coupling forces an architecture trade-off that shouldn't need to exist: you can organize your **repo** by medallion layer (`pipelines/01_bronze/`, `02_silver/`, `03_gold/`) AND get one DLT pipeline per layer chained by sequential job tasks — or you can get a single end-to-end DLT pipeline (no artificial job-task hops between layers) by giving every flowgroup the same `pipeline:` value — but then you lose all repo-level organization in the generated output, because everything collapses into one flat `generated/<env>/<pipeline>/` folder regardless of which source subfolder it came from.

## Concrete motivating scenario

Two source entities, medallion architecture:
- Bronze: entity A and entity B ingested 1:1 (no fan-in yet).
- Silver: entity A and entity B cleaned 1:1 (still no fan-in).
- Gold: A and B are joined/combined into one output.

Two ways to lay this out today, both with a real downside:

**A. One `pipeline:` value per layer** (`bronze`, `silver`, `gold`) — matches the folder structure (`pipelines/01_bronze/`, `pipelines/02_silver/`, `pipelines/03_gold/`), and each layer becomes its own DLT pipeline. You then chain the three with a Databricks Job with 3 sequential tasks (`lhp dag --format job`). Downside: this hard-splits the lakehouse into layers at the *job* level — one slow/stuck flow in bronze holds up the entire silver task from starting, even for the entity that had nothing to do with the slow flow, because the task boundary (not the DLT engine's real dependency graph) gates progress.

**B. One `pipeline:` value for everything** (e.g. `pipeline: all`) — every flowgroup across bronze/silver/gold becomes part of a single DLT pipeline. This is actually the *architecturally correct* choice for this scenario: DLT/Lakeflow's own dependency-resolution engine schedules each entity's bronze→silver chain independently and only serializes at the real data dependency (the gold join waiting on both silver outputs) — no artificial per-layer job-task gating. Downside: `generated/<env>/all/` now contains every flowgroup's `.py` file, flat, with zero trace of the bronze/silver/gold organization that still exists (and matters) in `pipelines/`. Same for `resources/lhp/all.pipeline.yml` — one resource file for the entire lakehouse.

```

resources/lhp/all.pipeline.yml
```

Issue #8562: [Bug] visit [-->] never terminates on cyclic graphs — osp_visit has no visited set

### What's wrong

`visit [-->]` on a graph with a cycle re-enqueues nodes unconditionally — traversal never terminates and burns CPU printing until killed. The OSP kernel's `osp_visit()` tracks only `scope.ignores`; there is no visited set. A self-loop is enough to hang any program.

### Minimal repro

```jac
# cycle.jac
node N { has tag: str; }
walker W {
    can start with Root entry { visit [-->]; }
    can go with N entry { print(here.tag); visit [-->]; }
}
with entry {
    a = N(tag="A");
    root ++> a ++> a;   # a has an edge back to itself
    root spawn W();
}
```

```
timeout 5 jac run cycle.jac
```

### Expected vs actual

Expected: each node visited once per traversal (or termination per documented revisit policy); program exits after printing `A`.

Actual: prints `A` thousands of times per second forever (killed via timeout after ~3400 lines in 5s). Any user graph containing a cycle makes `jac run` spin at 100% CPU with no diagnostic.

### Suggested direction

One coherent fix for the revisit question in `osp_kernel.jac` `osp_visit()`, not two ad-hoc rules:

- Track a per-traversal visited set of edge/node anchors so each node is enqueued once by default.
- Note the same mechanism currently dedupes duplicate parallel edges between the same pair, so whatever policy lands must preserve that behavior.
- If revisiting is ever wanted, make it explicit opt-in (e.g., a `visit` modifier), never implicit.

Related but distinct: #6636 covers the *native* stopgap gate where a node-in-list cycle guard silently evaluates False — this report is the kernel-level missing visited-set in dev-mode Python runtime.

### Environment

- jac 0.16.7 (dev mode), main@844ea3ea5
- Linux x86_64

Issue #4609: Property read cost depends on where the property sits in the record

## Problem

Two things about how a property is read make aggregation over a large expansion cost more than the data it returns.

**Read cost depends on where the property sits.** Fetching a property is not constant-time with respect to the record it lives in: a property stored later in the record costs measurably more to read than one stored earlier. On a node carrying eight properties, reading the last is around twice the cost of reading the first. Which properties are cheap is therefore an accident of the order they were first written, and users have no way to see or influence it.

**Nothing amortises across the properties a row actually reads.** A query reading three properties of one node pays three independent lookups, each starting from scratch. There is no cheaper path for "give me these three" than asking three times.

**Each value is built twice.** A read produces an intermediate representation which is then converted into the form the query evaluates. For a query over tens of millions of rows that is two constructions and two destructions per property per row, for values that are usually a number or a short string.

## Reproduction

1. Create nodes carrying 8 properties: a mix of strings, integers, doubles and a boolean.
2. Time `RETURN sum(n.first)` against `RETURN sum(n.last)` where `first` and `last` are the first and last properties written.
3. The second is materially slower, for identical work.
4. Time a query reading three properties against three queries reading one each; the combined cost is close to the sum, not below it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cost of reading a property does not depend on its position in the record
- [ ] Reading a set of properties of one node costs materially less than reading them one at a time
- [ ] A value is constructed once on the path from storage to expression evaluation

```text
source construction

  -> wasm32-wasip2 artifact
```

```yaml
source: {tree_sha256, file_manifest_sha256}
artifact: {wasm_path, wasm_sha256, size}
```

## Overview

Build a single "no-public-mutation oracle" for the no-publish rehearsal candidate required by #4350. A Boolean field like `publish_authorized: false` is not an oracle: a workflow can claim no-publish while still carrying effective release mutation authority. This issue requires executable proof of two things:

1. The rehearsal has **no effective authority** capable of public publication.
2. **No external tag/release/registry/Marketplace/container/package-channel state changed** during the run.

Scope guardrails: this issue changes no public channel and creates no release. Channel-specific publisher semantics remain with their existing owners (#7831 and existing registry/Marketplace/OpenVSX/container channel issues); this train composes them and does not create another publisher stack.

Context: parent issues #4350, #6055; ordering authority #6231; live controls #4145/#6230/#6241/#8551; topology #5889/#6052; package-channel state #7831; final publication #4351/#6070.

## Motivation

#6231 demonstrates why configuration review alone is insufficient: an irreversible publisher may already be dispatched before the build failure that should have blocked it. A workflow claiming no-publish may still carry:

- `contents: write` or effective release mutation authority;
- OIDC/attestation/write permissions;
- publisher secrets or inherited reusable-workflow secrets;
- an unconditional release/downstream publish dispatch;
- a `release: published` feedback path;
- a command whose dry-run flag is lost;
- a post-step that updates a public package channel;
- mutable container/package metadata.

#4350 requires:

```yaml
publish_authorized: false
published_channels: []
release_cut: false
```

## Authority preflight

Before candidate code or dependencies run, inspect the complete reachable workflow graph: event and inputs; called/reusable workflows; job/step permissions; environments; secret inheritance and named secret references; OIDC/id-token authority; GitHub token permissions; external publisher tokens; repository/workflow dispatch calls; shell/scripts/actions capable of tag/release/channel mutation; conditional expressions and failure paths.

Classify each reachable node:

```text
read_only
artifact_local_write
candidate_evidence_write
public_mutation_disabled
public_mutation_unreachable
public_mutation_authorized
not_proven
```

Any reachable `public_mutation_authorized` or `not_proven` node blocks the rehearsal.

## Public-state baseline and comparison

Record bounded before/after observations for every topology-relevant external surface:

- publication repository tags
- GitHub Releases and assets
- crates.io package versions
- VS Code Marketplace extension versions
- Open VSX extension versions
- container registry tags/digests when required
- Homebrew/Scoop/Chocolatey/WinGet or other required package-channel state
- downstream workflow dispatch/run identities

The surface set derives from `release_topology.v1`; deferred channels receive a topology-backed `not_applicable` row. A source workflow existing for a channel is not evidence that public state was unchanged — each observable must name its API/instrument state.

Run the exact no-publish candidate path with:

- immutable candidate SHA and packet digest;
- exact topology;
- no publisher environments or effective publisher secrets;
- local/staged package operations only;
- registry dry-runs only where genuinely non-mutating;
- no tag or GitHub Release creation;
- no downstream public refresh dispatch;
- no `release: published` event.

Every stage emits a typed receipt; missing or malformed stage evidence is `not_proven`.

Issue #5191: Reproducible label-aware augmentation artifacts in the computer-vision example

## Overview

Propose a small, self-contained example (or optional variant of the existing `examples/computer_vision` example) that makes a label-aware augmentation policy an explicit, versioned artifact in a ZenML computer-vision pipeline, using the `albumentationsx` package (imports as `albumentations`).

## Use Cases

- Reproducible object-detection pipelines: the augmentation policy and seed are part of the data lineage — changing either changes the training dataset even when the source dataset is unchanged.
- The current `examples/computer_vision` workflow (FiftyOne COCO export → Ultralytics training → model artifact versioning → inference → FiftyOne analysis) versions the exported dataset and model, but has no explicit augmentation-policy artifact or label-aware dataset-preparation step between them.
- Stochastic preprocessing needs sample-level randomness that stays stable regardless of sample or worker execution order.

## Proposed implementation

Bounded to two ZenML steps:

1. Build an AlbumentationsX pipeline and return `A.to_dict(pipeline)` as a normal ZenML `dict` artifact.
2. Reconstruct it with `A.from_dict()`, apply synchronized image and bounding-box transforms to the exported YOLO dataset, and return the resulting directory as a ZenML `Path` artifact for the existing trainer.

Core sketch:

```python
import albumentations as A

policy = A.Compose(
    [
        A.HorizontalFlip(p=0.5),
        A.RandomBrightnessContrast(p=0.2),
    ],
    bbox_params=A.BboxParams(
        coord_format="yolo",
        label_fields=["class_labels"],
    ),
)

policy_artifact = A.to_dict(policy)

# In the downstream dataset-preparation step:
policy = A.from_dict(policy_artifact)
sample = policy(
    image=image,
    bboxes=bboxes,
    class_labels=class_labels,
    invocation_seed=stable_sample_seed,
)
```

The sample seed is derived from a pipeline parameter and a stable sample identifier, so the generated dataset does not change merely because the orchestrator processes samples in a different order.

Resulting lineage:

```text
source dataset -> augmentation policy + seed -> transformed dataset -> trained model
```

No new ZenML integration, stack component, or custom materializer is needed — only existing materialization for `dict` and `Path`.

## Alternatives considered

- Leaving augmentation inside the training implementation: does not make the policy or transformed dataset separate lineage artifacts.
- A custom materializer for `A.Compose`: possible, but a serialized dict is simpler and uses existing ZenML primitives.
- Changing the current computer-vision example by default: unnecessarily disruptive; an optional step or separate example preserves the existing path.

## Constraints / dependency boundary

- Public `albumentationsx` package is AGPL-3.0-only; imports as `albumentations`.
- Importing it requires PyTorch, which is intentionally not pinned in its package metadata (users choose CPU/CUDA/MPS builds); the example would document that runtime choice rather than add a universal PyTorch pin.
- AlbumentationsX stays scoped to this example, not a ZenML runtime dependency.

## Priority

Low — nice to have. Contributor is willing to implement once maintainers confirm placement (optional branch of `examples/computer_vision` vs. standalone example).

Issue #1263: fix(core): agent_depth infinite loop on parent-chain cycles in persisted state

## Overview

`agent_depth` in `cadis-core/src/lib.rs:5705-5717` traverses the agent parent chain with an unguarded `while let` loop:

```rust
while let Some(parent_agent_id) = self.agents.get(current).and_then(|agent| agent.parent_agent_id.as_ref()) {
    depth += 1;
    current = parent_agent_id;
}
```

There is no visited-set check or depth limit. If persisted state is manually edited or corrupted such that agent parent references form a cycle (e.g., agent A's parent is B and agent B's parent is A), the loop never terminates.

## Pain

- Any request triggering `agent_depth` with a cyclic parent chain hangs the daemon indefinitely.
- While hung, the runtime mutex is held, blocking all other requests — effectively a denial-of-service triggered by corrupted state files.
- Such a hang is difficult to diagnose in production without inspecting state files directly.

## Use Cases

- Runtime computes `agent_depth` for an agent whose persisted parent chain contains a cycle: must not hang.
- State recovery (`recover_agent_records`) loads a state file containing cyclic parent references: cycle should be detected during recovery.

## Expected Behavior

- `agent_depth` handles cycles gracefully — either break the loop with a logged warning or cap the depth at a reasonable maximum — and the daemon never hangs due to corrupted agent parent references.

## Fix Requirements

1. Add a `HashSet<AgentId>` visited set to the loop; if `current` is already visited, break and log a warning about the cycle.
2. Alternatively, add a maximum depth limit (e.g., 100) as a safety guard.
3. Add cycle detection during state recovery (`recover_agent_records`).

## Notes

- Critical level: Low. Confidence: High — the code at `lib.rs:5705-5717` was deep-read and confirmed to contain no visited-set or depth-limit guard.

- 代码面板通过抽象 `Semantic Code Anchor` 实时高亮映射多语言（TypeScript/Go/Rust）代码与教学变量。

Issue #108: Long chain of external $ref files overflows the parser stack

## Overview

Parsing a JSON Schema whose `$ref`s form a long chain across many *external* files throws `StackOverflowError` — not during generation, but during parsing itself, before any value is ever attempted.

## Use Cases

- Large, modular schema suites split across many files that reference each other via relative-path external `$ref`s should parse regardless of how many files the chain spans.

### Minimal reproduction

A directory of files that each `$ref` the next by relative path:

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
N = 3000
for i in range(N):
    nxt = i + 1
    content = ('{"$ref": "f%d.json#/def", "def": {"type": "string"}}' % nxt
               if nxt < N else '{"def": {"type": "string"}}')
    open(f"f{i}.json", "w").write(content)
PY
```

`Gjuton.of(new File("f0.json"))` then throws `StackOverflowError` on a default-size JVM thread stack. A chain of ~1500 files does not yet trigger it, so the threshold is stack-size dependent, not schema-size dependent — the point is that no chain length is rejected gracefully.

## Current implementation

`SchemaParser.collectRefs`, in its external-`$ref` branch, recurses into itself for every newly-encountered external `$ref`, with no depth limit:

```java
var externalDoc = loadExternalDocument(baseUri, baseDir);
qualifyRefsWithinExternalDocument(externalDoc, baseUri);
refs.put(ref, resolveFragment(fragment, externalDoc));
collectRefs(externalDoc, externalDoc, refs, baseDir, baseUri);
```

Each hop to a new file is plain Java call-stack recursion. `RefGenerator` bounds recursive `$ref` resolution during *generation* via the context's hard depth limit, but nothing bounds it during parsing.

## Pain

- A schema legitimately split across enough files — a common pattern for large, modular schema suites — exhausts the JVM call stack and crashes with `StackOverflowError`.
- This is unrelated to the allOf-specific generation recursion fixed in #88: that failure needs mutually-recursive `$ref`s, this one needs only an ordinary non-cyclic chain of enough distinct files.

## Fix direction

A depth cap isn't right here: unlike generator-side chains (which really are cyclic/unsatisfiable past a small depth), a schema split across many files is not inherently invalid — capping depth would reject large-but-valid modular schemas. The more correct fix is to make `collectRefs`'s cross-file traversal iterative (an explicit work queue/stack) instead of Java call-stack recursion, so it isn't bounded by JVM stack size at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Parsing a schema whose `$ref`s form a long chain of external files succeeds (or fails with a clear, catchable exception) regardless of chain length

Issue #238: Consolidate VR performance settings into one place (DRY, single source of truth)

## Overview

VR stereo-reprojection performance settings are currently split across two tiers: the central G-buffer level control (`VRStereoOptimizations` — "Stereo Reprojection" mode combo in the VR feature panel) and per-effect controls inside individual features (SSS "VR Stereo Sync" + "VR Stereo Reprojection"; SSGI "VR Stereo Reprojection"). Each per-effect toggle is dev-mode-gated and only appears in its own feature's panel. A VR user hunting for perf toggles must visit every feature and enable developer mode. This issue proposes a structural consolidation: keep each toggle owned by its feature, but surface every VR perf toggle in a central VR panel section via a shared registry — one state, multiple views.

## Use Cases

- A VR user finds all stereo-reprojection perf toggles in one central panel without enabling developer mode.
- A user toggles the same setting contextually from the feature's own panel; the central panel reflects the change (single backing state, no drift).
- SSS/SSGI reprojection, now default-on for performance, can be disabled by normal users through a non-debug UI path.

## Principle: one state, multiple views

- Duplicating the *bool* is the anti-pattern (two states that drift).
- Duplicating the *view* is the pattern (two controls bound to one bool).
- Each toggle stays **owned by its feature** (single backing var — already true).
- It surfaces in **both** the feature's own panel (contextual) and a central VR panel section (discoverability), bound to the same state.

## Current implementation

- **G-buffer level (central):** `VRStereoOptimizations` — "Stereo Reprojection" mode combo in the VR feature panel.
- **Per-effect level:** SSS "VR Stereo Sync" + "VR Stereo Reprojection"; SSGI "VR Stereo Reprojection" — each gated behind `IsDeveloperMode()`, each only in its own feature's panel.
- Terminology was already unified in #236/#237 (all "Stereo Reprojection", "Eye 0 (left)/Eye 1 (right)").

## In-codebase precedent

- **`CSEditor` overlay analog:** the weather details window uses a `ShowInOverlay` bool + shared `Draw*()` functions rendered from both the settings menu and the in-world overlay — one widget, one state, two mount points. This issue generalizes that from one widget to a cross-feature registry.

## Design

1. **Descriptor + registry.** Each feature registers its VR-relevant toggles as `{ label, tooltip, bool* state, availability() }`. The central VR panel iterates the registry and renders each; the feature panel renders its own from the same descriptor. No hardcoded per-feature list in the VR panel; checkbox/tooltip/gate rendering written once (`Util::UI::DrawVRToggle(entry)`).
2. **Central VR panel section** in `VRStereoOptimizations` grouping the G-buffer "Stereo Reprojection" mode with the per-effect toggles.
3. **Graduate out of dev-mode.** Toggles go default-on for performance (measured: SSS -37% pipeline cost; SSGI GI-march -37/-43/-46%, up to 0.73ms at Reference), so users need a normal (non-debug) way to turn them off. Remove the `IsDeveloperMode()` gate as part of this.

5. **Mode-combo consolidation (optional, nice-to-have):** SSS's two mutually-exclusive checkboxes (Sync = reconcile both eyes; Reprojection = skip one eye) could become one combo [Off | Sync | Reprojection], matching the global combo shape. Needs a settings migration; can be a second step.

- Terminology (done in #236/#237).

Issue #9196: cargo-test aborts with a stack overflow on every PR — `statically_reachable_trusted_js_package_is_aot_compiled_without_route_entry`, and a Python-only diff reproduces it

## Overview

The `cargo-test` CI job is failing on **every** open PR with a **stack overflow** (SIGABRT), not an assertion failure:

```
thread 'commands::compile::collect_modules::tests::
        statically_reachable_trusted_js_package_is_aot_compiled_without_route_entry'
       (12606) has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
process didn't exit successfully: .../perry-c8602d85b11282cb (signal: 6, SIGABRT)
```

Because the abort takes down the whole test binary, every test that had not yet run is skipped — the same masking shape as #9108. The visible failure is one test; the cost is the tail of the run.

The failing test is `statically_reachable_trusted_js_package_is_aot_compiled_without_route_entry`, located at `crates/perry/src/commands/compile/collect_modules/tests.rs:604`, originating from #8529 (`fix(compile): AOT-promote trusted reachable JavaScript`). It long predates the affected PRs.

## Reproducibility — not caused by any diff

Confirmed on four PRs with unrelated contents, all the same test, all the same signal:

| PR | contents | cargo-test |
|---|---|---|
| #9190 | `perry-runtime` only | stack overflow |
| #9191 | codegen | stack overflow |
| #9185 | codegen | FAILURE |
| **#9193** | **`scripts/ci_e2e_scope.py` only — zero Rust** | **stack overflow** |

#9193 is decisive: it changes a single Python file, cannot affect the compiled test binary, and reproduces the abort identically. The cause is therefore on `main`.

## Known facts

- The test binary is a **debug** build (`target/debug/build/perry/...`), where stack frames are largest and no inlining trims recursion depth.
- Stack overflow (rather than assertion failure) points at unbounded or deep recursion in module collection / reachability walking, not at a wrong expected value.
- Not yet root-caused; a one-file Python PR (#9193) is a free reproducer for whoever picks this up.

## Pain

Two required gates are red on `main` at once — this one and `e2e-scoped` (fixed in #9193). A permanently-red required check teaches reviewers to merge past red, so the next real regression lands invisibly behind it. The stack-overflow shape is worse than a normal failure because it silently truncates the rest of the test suite.

## Suggested next steps

1. Confirm determinism: re-run `cargo test -p perry --bin perry statically_reachable_trusted` on `main` at `84185b5656` and check whether it aborts every time or intermittently. If intermittent, the trigger is likely test *ordering* or a shared fixture, not the test itself.
2. `RUST_MIN_STACK` bisection to determine recursion depth — whether it is deep-but-bounded (a threshold problem) or unbounded (a cycle in the reachability walk, e.g. a package graph that re-enters itself when a subpath resolves back to its own root).
3. If it is a cycle, the fix is a visited-set in the walk, and the regression test is the package shape that closes the loop.

## Overview

Introduce `ux_case_receipt.v2`, a versioned rich per-case receipt that is an internally coherent statement about **one exact executable case in one declared plan/run**. This PR owns only what the instrumented test itself directly observes: assertion outcomes, request/useful-result timing, bounded typed harness/protocol failure, case/target/test/plan/run identity, exact replay, and receipt write/validation state. It does not decide the case's operational role, quarantine, gate disposition, aggregate run verdict, or semantic repair owner — those policy joins are owned by #10020/#9908.

Relationships:
- Parent train: #9879
- Depends on stable case identity: #9890
- Consumes exact plan identity/role metadata: #10020
- Execution observer: #10022
- Finalizer consumer: #9908
- Current-main basis when rewritten: `2da40e518a9e48069f00b77f574f6c508888fa3b`

## Pain

The current receipt substrate is useful but can certify impossible or misleading states:

1. `finish_pass()` can serialize `result=pass` after a caller recorded a failed check and ignored the returned error.
2. Arbitrary `anyhow::Error` and panic paths collapse to `UxFailureClass::Unknown` even when the harness knows a bounded observable failure kind.
3. `failure_class` mixes observation with guessed product/test ownership and remediation routing.
4. Canonical replay is a package-wide substring filter, not exact target + exact full libtest name.
5. Friendly replay may not match a tested `just` interface.
6. Receipt identity lacks #9890 stable `case_id` and #10020 plan/profile identity.
7. Receipt write errors are swallowed, leaving later consumers unable to distinguish a clean uninstrumented pass from missing instrumentation.
8. Rust types, JSON schema, and manual validation arrays can drift as separate authorities.

## Use Cases

- Exact replay: reconstruct the exact `cargo` invocation (exact target + exact full libtest test name) and a friendly replay command matching a tested `just` interface.
- Downstream consumers (#9908) receive a semantically validated, unambiguous pass/fail statement with stable case and plan identity.

## Current implementation

- Recorder/taxonomy/runner: `crates/perl-lsp-ux-tests/src/recorder.rs`, `taxonomy.rs`, `run_ux_scenario`
- Schema checks: `crates/perl-lsp-ux-tests/schemas/ux-scenario-run.schema.json`, `tests/receipt_schema_validation.rs`

## Schema authority

Shared receipt types and semantic validation live in the existing `perl-lsp-ux-tests` library. Authority chain:

```text
Rust typed model
+ explicit semantic validator
        ↓
canonical JSON serialization
+ generated/checked external JSON-schema projection where retained
```

Requirements:
- No second hand-maintained field/enum list in `receipt_schema_validation.rs`.
- External JSON schema, if retained, is generated from or mechanically checked against the typed model plus semantic invariants.
- JSON Schema structural validity does not substitute for semantic validation.
- Unknown schema versions fail closed.
- Deterministic ordering and bounded payload fields are tested.
- Do not add another crate or generic repository schema framework solely for this receipt.

## Exact identity

Bind at least:

```text
schema/producer identity
case_id from #9890
target kind/name and full libtest test name
workflow/component display identity where applicable
#10020 plan digest, tier, feature profile, and operational role reference
repository SHA / dirty-state disposition
run ID / attempt / platform
receipt attempt identity where retry is explicitly modeled
```

The operational role may be copied as referenced context for review, but this receipt does not interpret it into pass/quarantine/gate semantics.

- Same case from another plan/run cannot be relabeled current.

Replace or supplement the current broad `UxScenarioResult`/`UxFailureClass` with a closed observable result vocabulary equivalent to:

```text
assertions_passed
assertion_mismatch
rpc_or_protocol_error
bounded_timeout
server_crash_observed
binary_or_spawn_unavailable
harness_fixture_or_environment_error
```

Issue #1: Feature: opt-in stacked merge requests for dependency work

## Overview

Add opt-in support for stacked merge requests in the dependency workflow. The feature must be disabled by default, operate only on the configured project repository, and never create branches, PRs, or perform work against `digitaldrywood/detent` as an upstream repository.

## Use Cases

- A dependent issue stays in `Todo` until all blockers are merged; then its branch is created from the remote default branch (`main`).
- When every blocker except exactly one is merged and the remaining blocker is in `Human Review`, the child branch is created from that blocker's branch (stacked), with the child PR initially targeting the parent branch.
- When the parent merges, the child branch is rebased/refreshed onto `main`, the child PR is retargeted to `main`, and normal checks/merge gates rerun.

## Configuration

Per-project/workflow setting:

```yaml
workspace:
  stacked_branches:
    enabled: false
```

Omitted and explicit `false` values must preserve current behavior. Configuration defaults to disabled and must validate correctly.

## Dispatch policy

Dependent issue may start only when:

1. Every blocker is merged → branch from remote default branch (`main`).
2. Every blocker except exactly one is merged, and the remaining blocker is in `Human Review` → branch from that blocker's branch.

Dispatch must NOT start when:

- two or more blockers are unmerged;
- the unmerged blocker is in `In Progress`, `Rework`, `Merging`, `Blocked`, or another non-review state;
- the `Human Review` blocker has no open, non-draft, non-merged PR and source branch;
- the parent branch is unavailable;
- dependency state changed between board refresh and workspace creation.

PR merge status is authoritative for code blockers. Non-code/no-PR blockers may continue using existing terminal-state rules.

Parent selection must be deterministic and revalidated immediately before workspace creation. If multiple blockers are in `Human Review`, do not choose arbitrarily; leave the child in `Todo`.

## Stacked branch behavior

For the single eligible `Human Review` parent:

- fetch and pin the parent branch head;
- create the child branch/worktree from that parent SHA;
- initially target the child PR at the parent branch;
- persist the parent issue, branch, and SHA;
- expose the relationship and wait reason in the UI, logs, and telemetry.

## Parent lifecycle

If the parent changes while the child is active:

- detect the parent branch head change;
- do not silently rewrite the child worktree;
- pause with an actionable `stack_parent_changed` condition;
- rebase in a controlled worker attempt before resuming;
- if the parent leaves `Human Review`, pause the child until it returns or merges.

When the parent merges:

1. fetch the current `main`;
2. rebase/refresh the child branch onto `main`;
3. retarget the child PR to `main`;
4. rerun normal checks and merge gates.

If the parent closes without merging, or its branch is deleted/unavailable, fail closed with an actionable Rework/Blocked reason. Never silently fall back to `main`.

Existing branches created with the wrong base must be preserved and explicitly reconciled; they must not be silently deleted, replaced, or rebased.

## Scope and safety

- Same-repository parents only.
- Validate branch/ref names and pass Git arguments without shell interpolation.
- Detect dependency cycles.
- Preserve all existing capacity, budget, authorization, CI, retry, and merge gates.
- No behavior change when the feature is disabled.

## Acceptance criteria

- Configuration defaults to disabled and validates correctly.
- All-merged dependencies create a branch from `origin/main`.
- Exactly one eligible `Human Review` dependency creates a branch from that parent.
- Multiple unmerged dependencies prevent dispatch.
- Missing/draft/closed/merged-parent cases follow the stated rules.
- Child PR base is initially the parent branch and becomes `main` after parent merge.
- Parent changes, deletion, closure, fetch failures, stale state, restart, and race conditions are handled deterministically.
- Parent metadata and dependency wait reasons are visible in UI, logs, and telemetry.
- Unit and integration tests cover dispatch, hydration, branch creation, PR targeting, re-anchoring, and failure recovery.

```rust
{
    let held_others = locks
        .borrow()
        .iter()
        .map(|(id, state)| (*id, state.type_name))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>();                       // allocates before any enabled check
    global_order::record_and_check(type_id, type_name, &held_others);
}

// :344-348 — both AFTER the collect
if held_others.is_empty() { return; }
if !ENABLED.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { return; }
```

Expose `global_order::is_enabled()` (or reuse `set_enabled_for_tests`' flag) and hoist both the emptiness and enabled test above the `collect`:

```rust
if locks.borrow().len() > 0 && global_order::is_enabled() { … }
```

Behaviour is identical — `record_and_check` already returns on both conditions — and the fast path then really is one relaxed load, as documented.

Issue #32: Limits

## Overview

Define deterministic rejection boundaries for hostile, malformed, or pathological semantic artifacts. The runtime accepts externally supplied semantic packages, catalogs, dependency graphs, execution requests, request bindings, provenance graphs, execution bundles, and ZIP archives — so resource behavior becomes part of portable verification.

Core principle: invalid or unsafe artifacts fail deterministically **before** uncontrolled resource exhaustion.

## Resource dimensions

Define deterministic limits or bounded algorithms for:

**Archives**
- maximum archive size
- maximum archive entry count
- maximum individual uncompressed entry size
- maximum total uncompressed size

**Semantics**
- maximum semantic assertion count
- maximum symbol count
- maximum identifier length
- maximum canonical value length
- maximum canonical line length

**Graphs**
- maximum models in dependency closure
- maximum dependency depth
- maximum derivation depth
- maximum relational dependency depth
- maximum provenance traversal depth

**Relational**
- maximum dataset rows
- maximum JOIN output occurrences
- maximum GROUP_BY coordinates
- maximum groups
- maximum aggregation contributions

**Execution**
- maximum execution request count
- maximum binding count

## Security cases

**Archive attacks:** ZIP bomb, path traversal, `../` entry, absolute path, duplicate normalized path, case-normalization collision where relevant, oversized member, excessive entry count.

**Semantic graph attacks:** dependency cycle, derivation cycle, dataset cycle, extreme dependency depth, extreme fan-out, extreme provenance expansion.

**Relational attacks:** intentionally explosive many-to-many JOIN, repeated Cartesian expansion, unbounded intermediate relation, aggregation over pathological cardinality.

**Canonicalization attacks:** extremely large identifiers, extremely large scalar values, oversized canonical serialization, pathological decimal representations.

## Failure timing

Reject unsafe structures as early as possible. Prefer:

- parse / structural verification before semantic execution
- closure validation before model evaluation

where possible.

## Interoperability

- Limits that affect whether an artifact is accepted must be part of a declared verifier profile. Two runtimes claiming the same profile should not disagree because one silently allows a vastly larger artifact.
- Resource limits must not affect semantic identity of valid artifacts — an artifact does not gain a different semantic identity merely because it is close to a verifier limit.

## Temporary resources

Verification and extraction must clean up temporary materialization after both success and failure. Core principle: safety policy constrains admissible execution; it does not rewrite semantic meaning.

## Acceptance criteria

1. ZIP traversal is rejected.
2. Absolute archive paths are rejected.
3. Duplicate normalized archive paths are rejected.
4. ZIP bombs are bounded.
5. Archive entry count is bounded.
6. Individual uncompressed size is bounded.
7. Total uncompressed size is bounded.
8. Dependency cycles are detected safely.
9. Dataset cycles are detected safely.
10. Provenance traversal is cycle-safe.
11. Deep semantic graphs cannot cause uncontrolled recursion.
12. Explosive JOIN cardinality has a deterministic bound or guarded execution policy.
13. Canonical resource limits are documented/profiled.
14. Failure occurs before expensive execution where possible.
15. Limits do not alter semantic identity of otherwise valid artifacts.
16. Equivalent implementations reject the same over-limit conformance fixtures.
17. Verification leaves no temporary materialization behind after failure.
18. Verification leaves no temporary materialization behind after success.

# package linking: propagate static-library native link requirements to final binaries

## What problem does this solve?

The SPEC explicitly says a dependency `staticlib` package's `(link ...)`
section is not propagated. Only the final binary package's link section,
source `extern` metadata, CLI inputs, and dependency archives reach the linker.

A TypeLisp wrapper around SQLite, raylib, an OS library, or a vendored C archive
therefore cannot be consumed compositionally. Every downstream executable must
know the wrapper's private implementation dependencies and copy its libraries,
search paths, and raw arguments. Platform fixes must be repeated in every
binary and can fail only at the final link with a poor undefined-symbol
diagnostic.

## Describe the solution

Define native link requirements as part of a static-library package's public
runtime interface and propagate them across its direct root edge to the final
executable link plan. #6966 forbids that wrapper from owning normal TypeLisp
package dependencies, but explicitly permits its native `(link ...)` metadata.

At minimum, the existing all-target and Linux/Windows `(link ...)` fields on a
`staticlib` should describe consumer requirements. If TypeLisp needs both
private build inputs and exported consumer requirements once more artifact
kinds exist, give that distinction explicit manifest syntax rather than
guessing from usage.

Relative search paths must be resolved against the declaring dependency root,
not the root binary's working directory. Merge order and duplicate handling
must be deterministic and preserve static-linker ordering constraints; do not
globally sort or deduplicate values when that changes linker meaning. The final
runtime-input sidecar and machine-readable metadata must include the declaring
package and effective ordered link plan so freshness and diagnostics remain
explainable.

## Project-goal justification

Practical systems packages are frequently safe TypeLisp APIs over native
libraries. TypeLisp already treats FFI and native archives as core systems
features; forcing every binary to understand wrapper linker internals makes
those packages substantially less usable and less portable than their source
API suggests. This can be fixed and dogfooded under exact pins without waiting
for external users or a registry.

## Selfhost implementation target

- manifest link semantics and dependency graph nodes
- ordered link-plan construction and platform selection
- artifact freshness/runtime-input sidecars and package metadata
- linker diagnostics with requirement provenance
- local/remote dependency integration gates for Linux and Windows
- SPEC §4.6 and docs/packages.md

## `get_n_hops_aconn(n)` is not shortest-path distance for `n > 2`

Comparing it against breadth-first search on `get_boolean_aconn()`:

```
off-diagonal entries where the two disagree: 11,798
of those, package reports SHORTER than the graph allows: 11,798

(package said, actually) -> count
  said 3, actually 4:            7,737
  said 4, actually 5:            3,027
  said 4, actually 6:              964
  said 4, actually no path <= 6:    70
```

Every disagreement is in the same direction.

### Cause

The recursion advances on the transitive closure rather than on the graph:

```python
c_prev_hops = np.copy(c)
for ih in np.arange(n_hops - 1):
    c_new = self._get_next_hop_aconn(c_prev_hops)
    c_prev_hops = c_prev_hops + c_new
```

`_get_next_hop_aconn` returns pairs exactly two hops apart *in whatever it is
given*. Given a two-hop closure that is up to four hops in the original graph,
so `n_hops=3` already contains pairs whose true shortest path is 4, and the
error compounds. The docstring says "Connectome n_hops away from the original
one", which a caller reasonably reads as graph distance.

If genuine n-hop reachability is intended, the recursion should compose the
current closure with the **original** adjacency rather than with itself.

### Reproduction

```python
import numpy as np, wormneuroatlas as wa
```

Issue #5: Road snapping can create disconnected anchors and stale span metadata

## Summary

`RoadSnapService` can modify an already generated road by truncating or snapping
its endpoint onto another road.

The resulting road geometry can become disconnected, while metadata derived
from the original geometry — especially bridge/tunnel spans — is not fully
recomputed for the modified road.

This can leave persisted `RoadData` internally inconsistent and produce visible
gaps or stale placement semantics during world generation.

## Observed behavior

While investigating a separate road-generation issue in a reproduced world
using seed:

`2823673442459948865`

a faulty road was found whose first persisted placement had been replaced by a
virtual anchor copied from another road.

The affected road started approximately like this:

```text
virtual anchor:
(666, 69, -669)

next real placement:
(699, 63, -689)
````

The distance between those positions was approximately:

`38.6 blocks`

No rasterized road segment connected the anchor to the next placement.

The virtual anchor matched an existing placement of another road and was
consistent with the behavior of shared-endpoint truncation in
`RoadSnapService`.

## Current behavior

The relevant lifecycle is approximately:

1. A road is generated.
2. Road segments and derived spans are computed.
3. `RoadData` is persisted.
4. Initial road post-processing can snap or truncate roads against each other.
5. `RoadSnapService` may:

   * replace an endpoint with a virtual anchor;
   * remove/truncate placements;
   * filter spans whose endpoints no longer exist.
6. Terrain-derived span information is not recomputed from the modified final
   geometry.

This means the geometry stored after snapping is not necessarily the geometry
for which the original spans were calculated.

## Disconnected anchor case

For the reproduced road, shared-endpoint truncation produced:

```text
existing road placement
        ↓
virtual anchor
        ↓
      38.6 block gap
        ↓
next actual RoadSegmentPlacement
```

Because there is no rasterized segment covering the gap, the physical road can
appear disconnected even though the persisted road logically begins at the
anchor.

`PathFeature` also ignores some placements near the beginning/end of a road,
which can make such endpoint gaps more visible.

## Stale metadata risk

Bridge and tunnel spans are derived before snapping modifies the final road
geometry.

After truncation, existing spans may be filtered when their endpoints were
removed, but the terrain classification is not recalculated for the resulting
road.

This creates a potential mismatch between:

```text
final RoadSegmentPlacement geometry
```

and:

```text
persisted RoadSpan metadata
```

Examples of possible consequences include:

* bridge spans beginning or ending at outdated positions;
* previously classified terrain no longer matching the snapped route;
* truncated roads containing gaps;
* materialization decisions being based on metadata from the pre-snap road.

## Expected behavior

After road snapping/truncation, persisted `RoadData` should remain internally
consistent.

A snapped connection should either:

* produce continuous road geometry between the new anchor and the remaining
  placements; or
* explicitly represent a valid discontinuity that downstream placement logic
  understands.

Any geometry-dependent metadata should correspond to the final geometry that
will actually be materialized.

## Actual behavior

`RoadSnapService` can modify the placement list after span extraction without
fully recomputing the derived geometry/terrain metadata.

In the reproduced case this resulted in a virtual anchor followed by an
approximately 38.6-block gap.

## Scope

This issue is specifically about consistency after road snapping/truncation.

It is separate from:

* coarse water classification;
* mod-biome compatibility;
* loss of water classification after precise path post-processing;
* bridge maximum-length handling;
* late planning / retrogen;
* map UI.

Issue #20903: Unmerged recursive CTE with UNION DISTINCT executes with UNION ALL semantics

### Overview of the Issue

A recursive CTE declared with UNION DISTINCT that does not merge into a single route silently executes with UNION ALL semantics. The planner records the distinctness on the operator (`operators.RecurseCTE.Distinct`), but it is only consumed when the whole CTE merges into one route (where the emitted SQL says `UNION DISTINCT` and MySQL deduplicates natively). When the CTE stays unmerged, `transformRecurseCTE` (`go/vt/vtgate/planbuilder/operator_transformers.go`) builds `engine.RecurseCTE` without it, no `Distinct` primitive is wrapped anywhere in the plan, and the engine primitive (`go/vt/vtgate/engine/recurse_cte.go`) has no accumulated seen-set in either the buffered or the streaming path — every term row is appended to the result and re-enqueued into the next generation.

The consequences versus MySQL are wrong row multiplicity on data that produces duplicate rows, and, on cyclic data, a `VT09030` recursion-limit error where MySQL terminates normally (MySQL's deduplication empties the working table; the engine's re-enqueue loop runs until `maxRecurseDepth`).

Possible directions are engine-side deduplication (which needs collation- and type-aware equality across the seed and every generation, in both execution paths, to match MySQL) or a planner-time unsupported error for the unmerged-distinct shape. The latter would reject queries that are accepted and executed today (and that return correct results on duplicate-free data such as strict hierarchies), so it would itself be a user-visible behavior change needing release-note treatment. Flagging it here so maintainers can pick the direction; noticed while working on #20631, which does not touch this code path.

### Reproduction Steps

Reproducible at the planner level against the planbuilder test vschema on current main:

1. Plan `with recursive cte as (select name, id from user where manager_id is null union select e.name, e.id from user e inner join cte on e.manager_id = cte.id) select name from cte` (the sharded join keeps the CTE unmerged).
2. Observe a plan containing `RecurseCTE` with no `Distinct` primitive anywhere, and a term query `select e.name, e.id from user as e where e.manager_id = :cte_id` — i.e. the DISTINCT of the union is gone.
3. Executing this against data where the term re-produces an already-seen row yields duplicates (or `VT09030` on cycles); MySQL deduplicates and terminates.

The merged case is correct: main's existing `cte_cases.json` golden "Merged recursive CTE with DISTINCT" pushes `UNION DISTINCT` into a single route.

### Binary Version

main (reproduced at 15366bf4b529; the engine primitive has never deduplicated).

### Operating System and Environment details

Not environment-specific; reproduced at the planner unit-test level.

### Log Fragments

None (wrong results; `VT09030: exceeded allowed recursion depth` in the cyclic case).

Issue #1523: the checker overflows its stack on a self-referencing typealias

Found while fixing #1521. **Reproduces on `main`.**

## The bug

```floe
typealias Tree = { l: Tree, r: Tree }
```

The checker recurses without a visited set and **overflows its stack**. The program never reaches codegen, so this is a crash rather than a miscompile.

## What it should do

Report a clear error naming the cycle. A `typealias` is structural, so a self-reference has no finite shape and cannot be resolved. A nominal `type Tree = { l: Tree, r: Tree }` is a different question and should keep working, because a nominal type is a name and the recursion terminates.

## Note

`#1521` added an alias walk in codegen that carries the open type names and stops on a repeat, so **codegen is already safe** if the checker is fixed. Whatever the checker does here, it will not be the thing that crashes.

## Tests

- A self-referencing `typealias` reports an error naming the cycle and does not crash.
- A two-step cycle, `typealias A = B` and `typealias B = A`, reports the same.
- A nominal `type Tree = { l: Tree, r: Tree }` still checks and builds.

Issue #29: Deduplicate and optimize the node execution plan

## Problem
`Script.CompileNodes()` builds `NodesToExecute` with a queue and `executionList.Contains(output)`. On converging graphs, a node can be enqueued more than once before it is added to the list, causing it to appear multiple times in the execution plan and potentially run multiple times in one cycle. The repeated linear `Contains` check also makes plan construction quadratic for larger graphs.

## Proposed work
- Build the reachable execution plan using a visited set marked when a node is enqueued.
- Preserve the current deterministic traversal order for valid acyclic graphs.
- Ensure each reachable node occurs exactly once in `NodesToExecute`.
- Add focused tests for fan-out/diamond graphs, including expected output and one-step execution behavior.
- Extend the benchmark suite with at least one converging graph scenario so scheduling overhead and regressions are measurable.

## Acceptance criteria
- A reachable node is executed at most once per `StepLine()` cycle.
- Valid disconnected nodes retain their current behavior.
- Execution-plan construction avoids repeated linear membership scans.
- Existing successful-script behavior remains unchanged.
- New tests and the full existing test suite pass.

Core desire is to strengthen relationships between tasks above/beyond what the existing pre/post functionality achieves; and to structure a nontrivial set of dependent state as a graph of tasks which only execute as many times as is required to set up that state.

Issue #104: # Roadmap 05 — Per-TS top-up: re-run one tilt-series without recomputing the job

**Status:** specified 2026-08-11, **not implemented**. Diagnosed from a live failure in
`/groups/klumpe/crboost_data/deadcode_test` (see §1). Companion to
[`../task-status-state-machine-roadmap.md`](../task-status-state-machine-roadmap.md), whose §5 record
migration this roadmap depends on for its phase 4 (the RUNNING claim) — see §6 for the coupling.

Unlike roadmaps 00–04 this one is **not** derived from the 2026-08-10 audit. It comes from a
reproduced production failure and fixes a capability gap, not a structural one.

## Before → After

**Before:** a tilt-series that fails one stage is silently dropped from that stage's output STAR and
therefore never appears in any downstream job's manifest. The array machinery to re-run *only* the
missing item already exists and is correct — but it is unreachable, because the code path that
preserves per-task status on re-run is gated on the job being `FAILED`, and a job that drops a TS
exits `SUCCESS`. The only available action is a full re-run of the job (and its whole downstream
chain) on a fresh job dir, recomputing every tilt-series that already succeeded.

**After:** "re-run tilt-series X through this job and everything after it" is a targeted action.
Partial success is a first-class outcome; the existing sparse-dispatch machinery is reachable;
un-excluding a muted TS actually brings it back. **Gain:** on a 60-TS dataset, recovering one bad
alignment costs one task instead of sixty, and the downstream chain tops up instead of recomputing.

---

## 1. The failure (reproduced, with evidence)

**Project:** `/groups/klumpe/crboost_data/deadcode_test` — 6 tilt-series, EER, `angpix 1.55`.

| Job | Type | Exit | `.task_status/` contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `External/job002` | fsMotionAndCtf | `RELION_JOB_EXIT_SUCCESS` | 6 × `.ok` — all 6 TS in `fs_motion_and_ctf.star` |
| `External/job004` | tsAlignment | **`RELION_JOB_EXIT_SUCCESS`** | 5 × `.ok` + **`deadcode_test_Position_1_3.fail`** |
| `External/job005` | tsCtf | `RELION_JOB_EXIT_SUCCESS` | **5 items — `Position_1_3` absent entirely** |

`Position_1_3` failed to align. `job004` exited SUCCESS anyway, by design —
`drivers/ts_alignment.py:276-277`:

```python
aligned_ts = results.ok
excluded_ts = sorted(results.failed + results.missing)
```

with the rationale in the comment above it: *"Per-TS alignment failure is normal in cryo-ET — AreTomo
simply can't solve every tilt-series. One bad TS must NOT abort the whole job and halt the pipeline
… Only a total wipeout (nothing aligned) is fatal."* **That policy is correct and must be kept.**

The consequence is the part to fix. `job004` emits a 5-TS `aligned_tilt_series.star`. Every
downstream job derives its manifest from its input STAR via
`read_tilt_series_names_from_input_star()`, so from `job005` onward `Position_1_3` is not a *failed*
item — it does not exist. Nothing downstream can retry what it has never heard of.

> **Do not confuse this with the orphan-marker bug** fixed on 2026-08-11 in the same project.
> `Position_1_2` in `job002` carried both `.ok` and `.fail` because a superseded array's orphan task

## 2. Why it cannot be retried today

The sparse re-dispatch itself is **already built and correct** —
`drivers/array_job_base.py:608-609`:

```python
previously_done = get_previously_done(job_dir)          # {.ok} | {.skip}
indices_to_run = [i for i, ts in enumerate(ts_names) if ts not in previously_done]
```

Re-running `job004` in place would re-align `Position_1_3` and nothing else. The blocker is that

Issue #353: HIER: external validation — real ontologies at scale, PLL baseline, Neo4j/TigerGraph and TimescaleDB comparisons

## Summary
The HIER benchmark added in #344 runs on a **generated** dataset so it is reproducible from a clean checkout with no download and no licence gate. That covers the *shapes* — tree and multi-parent DAG, subtree sizes spanning four orders of magnitude — but it does not establish the constants on real data, and it has no cross-engine baseline at all. `benchmarks/hier/README.md` lists these under "Not yet covered"; this issue is that list, made actionable.

## 1. Real ontologies at scale
`examples/ontology_loader.rs` already reads the published formats — OBO, NCBI `nodes.dmp`, GeoNames `hierarchy.txt`, prefix-coded (ATC, MITRE ATT&CK), generic edge lists, generated calendar — and reports the probe verdict, encoding, space and build time. What is missing is running it on the full files and recording the numbers.

Targets, and what each is expected to show:

| Source | Size | Expected verdict |
|---|---|---|
| NCBI Taxonomy | ~1.3M nodes | tree → nested-set; the scale case for build time and 12 B/node |
| GeoNames hierarchy | ~330k | tree → nested-set |
| ATC | ~6.5k | strict 5-level tree; the clean prefix case |
| MONDO / HPO | ~25k / ~19k | mostly tree, some multi-parent |
| **Gene Ontology** | ~50k | **declines** — width approaches leaf count |
| MITRE ATT&CK + CWE | ~1k / ~1.4k | tree via prefix / edge list |

The Gene Ontology row is the one to publish loudest. A high-width DAG is where a 2-hop index is the right structure and OEH refuses to build, and reporting that on the real file is more credible than any speedup. Verified on a GO-shaped synthetic (width 500 > cap 179); the real file has not been run.

Licence note: everything above is open. UMLS/SNOMED stay behind `--i-have-a-licence` and no ontology data gets committed.

## 2. PLL / 2-hop baseline
The paper's claim is ~half the space and 6–7× faster build than 2-hop labelling *at query parity* on trees. Samyama has no PLL implementation, so this is **not reproduced** — `benchmarks/hier/README.md` says so. The reference repo `relationship-hierarchy-index` has a validated PLL in Python; porting it as a benchmark-only baseline (not engine code) would let us make or retract the claim on our own data.

This also matters for the decline path: above the width cap we tell users to go to a 2-hop index, and we should be able to show what that costs.

## 3. Cross-engine: Neo4j / TigerGraph
The corpus is Cypher and the dataset is generated, so porting the loader plus the H1–H8/H10 queries is mechanical. Home is `samyama-graph-competitor-benchmarks`. Worth doing precisely because the interesting classes are the ones where we are *not* obviously ahead (H1, H4, H6) — an external number tells us whether those are a Samyama planner problem or inherent to the shape.

## 4. TimescaleDB continuous aggregates for H10
The paper's head-to-head: the reference implementation matches TimescaleDB continuous aggregates to the unit (day 704,800; month 21,168,000) while also answering subsumption, which a continuous aggregate cannot. HIER class H10 is the same workload but has only been compared against Samyama's own expansion. Reproducing the TimescaleDB comparison in-engine would let us state the roll-up claim against the incumbent rather than against ourselves.

## Definition of done
`benchmarks/hier/README.md` "Not yet covered" shrinks, with committed CSVs for whatever was run and an explicit note for anything that stays unrun and why.

Issue #434: [GAP-20] Provide a Prometheus exporter and tracing hooks

**Risk for enterprise users:** Low to Medium
**Labels:** `enhancement`, `feature-gap`, `area/observability`
**Reference implementations:** client-go `metrics/metrics.go` (Prometheus collectors), client-java `org/tikv/common/MetricsServer.java`, client-rust `src/stats.rs`

#### What is missing

`MetricsInterface` defines six hooks — `rpcStarted`, `rpcCompleted`, `retryAttempted`, `regionCacheHit`, `regionCacheMiss`, `regionInvalidated` (`src/Client/Observability/MetricsInterface.php:20-68`) — with an in-memory recorder and a no-op default. There is no Prometheus or StatsD adapter shipped, and no tracing integration at all.

#### How the official clients do it

client-go registers roughly a hundred Prometheus collectors covering command latency, backoff, region cache, and batch send tail latency (`metrics/metrics.go:41`), and supports OpenTracing spans (`internal/logutil/tracing.go:40-53`, gated by `config.OpenTracingEnable`) plus a newer pluggable structured trace-event layer with categories `CategoryTxn2PC`, `CategoryTxnLockResolve`, `CategoryKVRequest` and `CategoryRegionCache` (`trace/trace.go:27-45`). Note that client-go uses OpenTracing, not OpenTelemetry — `go.opentelemetry.io` does not appear in its `go.mod`. client-java ships an HTTP Prometheus exporter (`org/tikv/common/MetricsServer.java`) plus slow-log spans. client-rust has Prometheus histograms in `src/stats.rs` but no span tracing.

#### Impact of not having it

Every adopter writes the same adapter. More importantly, the metric set is thin: there is no backoff-duration histogram, no per-store error breakdown, and no lock-resolution or 2PC-phase timing, so an operator cannot tell from metrics alone whether latency is coming from PD, from a slow store, or from lock contention. This lengthens incident diagnosis but does not break anything.

The interface design itself is good and is genuinely ahead of client-rust in terms of pluggability — the gap is the shipped implementations and the metric coverage.

#### Workaround available today

Implement `MetricsInterface` against the organisation's metrics library — this is straightforward and the interface is well documented. The `SlowLogConfig` mechanism (`src/Client/Grpc/SlowLogConfig.php:15`) already provides per-operation slow-query logging, which covers part of the tracing need.

#### Implementation sketch

Ship an optional `PrometheusMetrics` adapter in a separate suggested Composer package to avoid a hard dependency. Extend `MetricsInterface` with backoff duration, per-store outcome, lock-resolution count and 2PC phase timings — noting that adding methods to a published interface is a breaking change, so consider a second interface or default implementations. For tracing, add a minimal span callback interface mirroring client-go's `TraceEventFunc` so callers can bridge to OpenTelemetry themselves.

#### Effort estimate

Small for the Prometheus adapter; Medium if the metric set is broadened and a tracing hook is added.

#### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Prometheus adapter is available without adding a hard dependency to the core package.
- [ ] Backoff duration, per-store outcomes and lock-resolution counts are recorded.
- [ ] 2PC phase timings (prewrite, commit) are recorded.
- [ ] A tracing callback interface exists and is documented with an OpenTelemetry example.
- [ ] Adding metrics does not break existing `MetricsInterface` implementations.

Issue #505: PRD: Parent Tasks, hierarchy, and leaf-first execution

## Problem Statement

Glasswork represents every vault work record as a **Task**, but its behavioral Task types do not preserve enough hierarchy or make the current execution level obvious. Today, ADO Product Backlog Items, User Stories, Features, and Epics all normalize to `type: pbi`. The UI therefore cannot reliably distinguish their exact source kind, Task Detail does not clearly identify containers, and deep ADO hierarchy is flattened.

This is most painful during day-to-day work. Execution, Notes, Artifacts, PRs, and agent traces usually belong to actionable leaf Tasks, while larger work should provide context, decomposition, coordination, and a current rollup. The current Task Detail page also renders the primary ADO Link twice, often shows a raw Parent ID instead of a title, and may open only ADO even when the Parent exists in Glasswork.

## Solution

Replace the behavioral `pbi` type with **Parent Task** and separate behavior from source presentation:

- `type: task` — actionable leaf; may own inline Subtasks.
- `type: bug` — actionable leaf; may own inline Subtasks.
- `type: parent` — non-leaf container; may own cross-file child Tasks and may not own inline Subtasks.
- `source_kind` — optional open display string preserving the exact imported ADO kind, such as `Epic`, `Feature`, `Product Backlog Item`, `User Story`, `Task`, or `Bug`. It never controls behavior.

Parent Tasks may nest to any acyclic depth. A Task has at most one Parent. Only Parent Tasks may own cross-file child Tasks. Local Parent relationships use the Parent's canonical Glasswork Task ID; unresolved external ADO parents remain explicit external references until their local Parent is available.

The UI stays leaf-first. Parent Tasks provide hierarchy, coordination, rollup, and lifecycle context without making container dates or priority silently change leaf actionability.

## User Stories

1. As a user opening Task Detail, I want the exact ADO source kind visible immediately, so that I can distinguish a Feature, PBI, Task, or Bug.
2. As a user opening a child Task, I want a named ancestor breadcrumb and an in-app Parent action, so that I can move through the Glasswork hierarchy without reconstructing it from ADO numbers.
3. As a user, I want the primary ADO work item shown once in Work hierarchy, so that Links can focus on PRs and other supporting evidence without duplication.
4. As a user, I want Parent Tasks to contain child Tasks rather than inline Subtasks, so that execution, Notes, Artifacts, and agent work remain attached to full leaf Tasks.
5. As a user, I want Parent Tasks to contain other Parent Tasks, so that Epic → Feature → PBI → task and native planning structures remain intact.
6. As a user, I want a Parent's child activity summarized without requiring every child agent to update each ancestor, so that Parent context stays current without distributed write coordination.
7. As a user, I want Parent Start/Resume/Wrap up actions to orchestrate descendants, so that familiar lifecycle verbs can coordinate child Tasks and sessions.
8. As a user, I want My Day to group leaves under their nearest Parent while preserving higher ancestry in a breadcrumb, so that I retain context without scanning nested container walls.
9. As a user explicitly coordinating a Parent today, I want a compact pinned Parent coordination row even when no child leaf is in My Day.
10. As a user scanning Backlog, I want an expandable hierarchy mode in addition to existing flat and board modes.
11. As a user choosing a Task in a search dialog, I want its kind badge and nearest Parent visible, with full ancestry available on demand.
12. As a user migrating existing PBIs, I want every inline Subtask promoted to a child Task without losing status, Notes, due/My Day state, size, or order.

## Domain Model

### Parent Task

A **Parent Task** is a Task with `type: parent`. It is a declared container role, not a role inferred from whether children happen to exist.
